_about.purpose: Typical plans keyed by PAWN STRUCTURE, not by opening name. One entry covers every ECO code that reaches the structure.
_about.provenance: Hand-authored from standard positional chess literature (Pachman, Soltis 'Pawn Structure Chess', Watson). This is curated human knowledge, NOT a downloaded data set and NOT LLM-generated at runtime -- see SOTA.md 2.5 for why no open data set of opening plans exists.
_about.owner_semantics: 'owner' is the side that owns the named feature: the IQP holder, the side playing the minority attack, the side with the bind.

Carlsbad.summary: White has traded the c-pawn for Black's e-pawn. The centre is fixed: White d4 against Black d5, Black's c-pawn faces a half-open c-file for White.
owner_plans: The minority attack: play b4-b5, trading b5xc6 to leave Black with a backward c-pawn on a half-open file.
Prepare it with Qc2, Rab1 and a4 before committing the b-pawn.
Alternatively play in the centre with f3 and e4, since Black's pieces are often committed to the queenside.
opponent_plans: Counterattack on the kingside, where you hold the extra central pawn and more space.
Play for the ...c5 break to free the position before the minority attack lands.
Meet b4-b5 with ...a6 or ...c6xb5 followed by piece pressure down the c-file.
good_pieces: The owner's light-squared bishop on f5/g4 or the knight heading to e5.
For the defender, a knight on e4 is a fine blockader.
bad_pieces: The defender's queen bishop is often passive behind the d5 pawn.
A knight on c6 can become a target once the minority attack lands.
typical_mistakes: Launching b4-b5 before the rooks and queen support it, so the pawn is simply lost.
As the defender, allowing the c-pawn to become backward without generating kingside play in return.
traps: After an early ...Ne4 the defender must be sure the knight cannot be chased with f3 and then punished on the e-file.

Isolated queen's pawn.summary: One side holds a d-pawn with no neighbours. It grants space, two open files and active pieces now, and becomes a weakness once pieces come off.
owner_plans: Play for the d4-d5 (or ...d5-d4) break, which liquidates the weakness at the best moment.
Attack: the isolated pawn buys the e5 and c5 outposts and open c- and e-files for the rooks.
Keep pieces on. Every exchange helps the blockader, so avoid trading queens.
Aim the light-squared bishop at h7 and lift a rook to the third rank.
opponent_plans: Blockade the pawn with a knight on the square directly in front of it.
Trade pieces. The endgame is where the isolated pawn is simply weak.
Pile up on the pawn with rooks and queen once it can no longer advance.
good_pieces: For the owner: knights on e5/c5 and both bishops pointing at the enemy king.
For the defender: the blockading knight in front of the pawn is the best piece on the board.
bad_pieces: The owner's rooks are poor if they end up defending the pawn instead of attacking.
typical_mistakes: The owner trading into an endgame, converting dynamic play into a static weakness.
The defender grabbing material on the queenside while the attack arrives on the kingside.
Pushing the isolated pawn as an attack rather than as a liberating break.
traps: The classic sacrifice on h7 works exactly when the defender has removed a kingside defender to blockade.

Hanging pawns.summary: Pawns abreast on the c- and d-files with no neighbours. They control key central squares while they stand, and become two weaknesses the moment one has to advance.
owner_plans: Keep them abreast as long as possible and use the space they grant.
Advance one at the right moment (usually d5 or c5) to open lines while the pieces are best placed.
opponent_plans: Provoke one to advance, then occupy the hole the advance leaves behind.
Pressure both on the half-open files and force a concession.
good_pieces: Pieces behind the pawns, ready to support a break.
bad_pieces: Any piece tied to passively defending one of the two pawns.
typical_mistakes: Advancing a hanging pawn without a concrete follow-up, creating a permanent hole.

Maroczy bind.summary: Pawns on c4 and e4 clamp the d5 square. The bound side has less space but a solid position and one clear freeing break.
owner_plans: Restrain. Avoid unnecessary trades, since each exchange eases the cramped side.
Build up slowly with Be3, Rc1, f3, and only then expand.
Meet the ...b5 break with careful preparation, never with panic.
opponent_plans: Fight for the freeing breaks ...b5 and ...d5, which are the whole point of the position.
Trade minor pieces: a cramped position improves with every exchange.
Use the half-open c-file for pressure against c4.
good_pieces: The binding side's dark-squared bishop and any knight reaching d5.
bad_pieces: The bound side's pieces without squares, especially a passive bishop on e7.
typical_mistakes: Sitting passively as the bound side and never fighting for a break.

Closed pawn chain.summary: Interlocking chains fix the centre. Play flows to the wings: each side attacks the base of the opposing chain.
owner_plans: Attack on the side where your chain points, typically the kingside, with f4-f5.
Gain space and restrict the defender's counterplay before opening a file.
opponent_plans: Strike at the base of the chain with ...c5 (and later ...f6), where your own chain points.
Solve the problem of the queen bishop, the piece the structure hems in most.
good_pieces: Knights routed to the strong square in front of the enemy chain's base.
bad_pieces: The defender's light-squared bishop, buried behind its own pawns.
typical_mistakes: Playing on the wrong wing: attacking where your chain does not point.
Releasing the tension in the centre too early and handing the opponent open lines.

King's Indian chain.summary: The centre is locked by d5/e4 against e5/d6. Both sides attack on opposite wings and speed matters more than material.
owner_plans: Play on the queenside with c4-c5, opening the c-file where your space advantage lies.
Do not be distracted by the kingside: race, and count tempi rather than pawns.
opponent_plans: Attack on the kingside with ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5-g4, aiming the pieces at the king.
Reroute the f6 knight so the f-pawn can advance.
good_pieces: The dark-squared bishop on g7, once the centre opens or the e5 pawn advances.
bad_pieces: Any piece defending on the wrong wing while the other side races.
typical_mistakes: Playing slowly. In mutual-attack structures a lost tempo is worth more than a pawn.

Open Sicilian.summary: White has traded the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn. Each side gets a half-open file aimed at the other's position: White down the d-file, Black down the c-file. Sharp, asymmetrical, and decided by who attacks faster.
owner_plans: Castle queenside and storm the kingside with f3, g4 and h4 while Black is slower.
Use the half-open d-file to press against the backward d6 pawn.
Fight for the d5 square: a knight or bishop landing there is often decisive.
Consider the Bg5 and f4 setup to provoke weaknesses before Black is ready.
opponent_plans: Attack down the half-open c-file, doubling rooks and aiming at c3 and c2.
Play ...b5-b4 to drive the c3 knight away and win the fight for d5.
Prepare the ...d5 break, which frees the position in one move if it works.
Do not defend passively: this structure rewards counterattack, not caution.
good_pieces: Any knight that reaches d5 for White, or c4 for Black.
The dark-squared bishops, which point straight at the opposing king.
bad_pieces: Black's d6 pawn is the standing weakness and whatever must defend it.
A white knight on d4 that has run out of squares once ...b5-b4 lands.
typical_mistakes: Playing slowly on either side: this is a race, and a tempo is worth more than a pawn.
As Black, grabbing the b2 pawn with the queen and losing the thread of development.
As White, opening the position while the king is still in the centre.
traps: The queenside pawn storm can rebound badly if the c-file opens before White's king finds shelter.
Watch the e6 and d5 squares: a sacrifice on either is the standard way this structure explodes.

Small centre.summary: A modest, flexible pawn centre on d6 and e6. Solid and free of weaknesses, but passive if the freeing breaks never come.
owner_plans: Prepare ...d5 or ...b5 at the right moment.
Complete development before opening the position.
opponent_plans: Take space and prevent the freeing breaks.
Consider a kingside pawn storm while the centre stays closed.
good_pieces: Knights on d4 and f3 for the space-holder.
bad_pieces: The cramped side's bishops before a break is achieved.
typical_mistakes: Never playing the freeing break and drifting into a passive position.

Open centre.summary: The central pawns are gone. Development, king safety and open files decide everything, and slow moves are punished immediately.
owner_plans: Develop quickly, castle, and seize the open files with the rooks.
Look for tactics: open positions favour the better-developed side.
opponent_plans: The same. Whoever finishes development first has the advantage.
good_pieces: Rooks on open files; bishops on long diagonals.
bad_pieces: An uncastled king; any undeveloped piece.
typical_mistakes: Making pawn moves instead of developing.
Leaving the king in the centre.

Symmetrical.summary: Mirrored pawns. The advantage lies in the extra tempo and in who breaks the symmetry on favourable terms.
owner_plans: Improve the worst-placed piece and avoid weakening the structure first.
opponent_plans: Equalise by copying only as long as it is safe, then find an independent plan.
good_pieces: Whichever piece has more squares than its counterpart.
bad_pieces: Any piece worse than its mirror image.
typical_mistakes: Breaking the symmetry without a concrete reason, which usually just creates the first weakness.

Unresolved centre.summary: The central tension has not been resolved. Who releases it, and when, will define the whole middlegame.
owner_plans: Finish development before resolving the tension.
Keep the option of several structures for as long as possible.
opponent_plans: The same: whoever resolves the tension first usually concedes a small concession.
good_pieces: Flexible pieces not yet committed to one structure.
bad_pieces: Pieces committed to a plan the centre may not deliver.
typical_mistakes: Releasing the central tension to gain a tempo and handing over a better structure.
